# Individual Grünbaum efficiency at an exposed deepest base

This is a local positive result for the boundary-potential route. It does not assert that a deepest point, or one of the fixed face witnesses, has an exposed base. In particular it does not settle the remaining witnesses in nonexposed faces.

## 1. Precise setting and statement

Let `d>=1`, let `P` be a nonempty finite set in `R^n`, and let every `K_z`, `z in P`, be a full-dimensional convex body in `R^d`. Set

    S=union_(z in P) ({z} times K_z),
    mu(E)=sum_(z in P) |E_z|,
    eta=sum_(z in P) H_(d-1)|boundary K_z.

The normal bundle uses the outward unit normal `n_z(x)`, defined for `H_(d-1)`-almost every boundary point. For `d=1` this is the two endpoints with their outward signs and counting measure. The raw mixed halfspace depth is denoted `D_S(z,x)`, with closed ambient halfspaces and the measure `mu`. Write `D_K(x)` for the ordinary raw depth in a single body.

Suppose `p` is an exposed vertex of `conv P`: there is a linear functional `ell` with

    ell(p)=0, ell(z)<0 for every z in P\{p}.

An additive constant is understood in this notation. The singleton case is included separately, with `ell=0` and no off-base conditions. Suppose `Y=(p,y)` is a global deepest point of `S`, of raw depth `Q`.

**Theorem.** The following assertions hold.

1. `D_S(p,x)=D_(K_p)(x)` for every `x in K_p`. Consequently `y` is an ordinary deepest point of `K_p`, lies in its interior, and

       Q>=Gamma_d |K_p|, Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.

2. Every ambient halfspace attaining depth `Q` at `Y` has a nonzero continuous normal, has its boundary through `Y`, captures exactly `Q` from `K_p`, and captures zero `d`-volume from every other fiber.

3. There is a finite positive circuit of depth-attaining caps whose continuous normals balance, whose restrictions cover the whole `p`-fiber plane, and which strictly miss all other fibers. Its own cuts are proper. All its cap-mass first derivatives exist, and each full mixed section has centroid `Y`. Thus this circuit has no supporting-face allocation ambiguity.

4. For any normalized nonnegative mixture `W=sum_j theta_j 1_(H_j)`, `sum theta_j=1`, of actual depth-attaining caps at `Y`, there is a nonnegative normal-dependent convex potential `Phi` with

       integral Phi d eta=1,
       integral Phi W d eta=Q/|K_p|>=Gamma_d.          (1)

The same conclusion holds if the profile is modified arbitrarily on other fibers, including by supporting-face allocations, because this potential is zero there.

Convex compatibility of the fibers is permitted but unnecessary for this exposed-base lemma. No analogous conclusion for an interior base is asserted.

## 2. Exact depth isolation and ordinary attainment

Any containing ambient halfspace restricts on the `p`-fiber either to an ordinary containing halfspace or to the whole fiber. Therefore its total mass is at least `D_(K_p)(x)`.

Conversely, fix an ordinary halfspace `u.v>=c` containing `x`, with `u!=0`. The ambient halfspace

    u.v+L ell(z)>=c

has the same trace on `K_p`. Since the other fibers are compact, their number is finite, and their `ell` values are strictly negative, a finite sufficiently large `L` makes this halfspace strictly disjoint from every other fiber. Its mass is exactly the ordinary captured mass. Taking infima proves the depth identity.

For a convex body, the function

    (u,x) -> |K intersect {v:u.(v-x)>=0}|, ||u||=1,

is continuous: the indicators converge off a hyperplane of Lebesgue measure zero, so dominated convergence applies. Its minimum over the compact unit sphere is continuous in `x`. Thus ordinary depth attains its maximum on `K`. A boundary point has zero depth, since a supporting halfspace captures only a boundary face of zero `d`-volume. The ordinary centroid has positive depth, at least `Gamma_d|K|`, by the classical continuous Grünbaum inequality. Hence every ordinary deepest point is interior.

The mixed global maximum at `Y` dominates the maximum of `D_(K_p)`, while the depth identity gives the reverse inequality at `y`. This proves part 1. Opposite halfspaces through an interior point have complementary volumes (their common hyperplane is null), so always

    0<Q<=|K_p|/2.                                    (2)

Now let an ambient containing halfspace have total mass `Q`. Its own trace has mass at least `Q`; thus it has exactly that mass, and all other traces have zero volume. A zero continuous normal would capture all of `K_p`, contradicting (2). If its boundary did not pass through `Y`, moving it parallel until it did would remove a positive own-fiber slab near the interior point `y`, contradicting the lower bound `Q` for all own containing halfspaces. Thus its boundary passes through `Y`, and its own trace is proper and positive. This proves part 2, without assuming regularity on other fibers.

## 3. Proper cuts are differentiable without smoothness of the body

We record the elementary regularity used to choose the circuit. For a full-dimensional convex body `K` and a hyperplane meeting its interior, the cap-volume map is continuously differentiable in its threshold and nonzero normal. Its derivatives are the usual section mass and first moment, divided by the normal length.

To prove this locally, choose coordinates so the given normal is `e_d`. Write vertical fibers of `K` as intervals `[l(x'),r(x')]` over its compact projection. For a nearby hyperplane `x_d=b-v.x'`, the captured fiber length is

    [r(x')-max(l(x'),b-v.x')]_+.

This is Lipschitz in `(v,b)` with an integrable uniform bound because the projection is compact. Except where the hyperplane meets `boundary K`, its derivative is either zero or `v_dot.x'-b_dot`, according as the cut misses or properly crosses the vertical interval. The exceptional set has `(d-1)`-measure zero: for a hyperplane meeting `int K`, its section has nonempty relative interior, and every point in that relative interior belongs to `int K`. Indeed, a supporting plane at a contrary point would have to contain the section plane, and would then contradict the interior crossing. The section boundary has zero relative measure. Dominated convergence gives both the derivative and its continuity under nearby proper cuts.

This proof also covers `d=1`, where a proper threshold is an interior point of an interval and the two endpoints are irrelevant to the local derivative.

For a through-`y` proper cap with normal `u`, variation of the normal by `w` has derivative

    (1/||u||) integral_(K intersect {u.(x-y)=0}) w.(x-y) dH_(d-1).  (3)

If it attains the minimum over all unit normals, (3) is zero in every tangent direction. The section displacement from `y` is perpendicular to `u`, so its centroid must be exactly `y`.

## 4. A finite regular isolated circuit

Let `U` be the set of unit normals of ordinary depth-attaining caps at `y`. It is nonempty and compact. We claim `0 in conv U`.

Otherwise strict separation gives a direction `v` and `epsilon>0` with `u.v>=epsilon` for every `u in U`. Move the candidate source to `y-tv`, with small `t>0`. The threshold derivative of every active cap is positive, since its section mass is positive and the threshold moves by `-t u.v`. By the continuous differentiability just proved, compactness gives a neighborhood of `U` and a uniform strictly positive first-order increase there. Outside this neighborhood the original cap masses exceed `Q` by a positive compactness gap. Uniform continuity preserves that gap for small `t`. Thus the depth strictly increases, contrary to ordinary maximality. This proves the claim.

Carathéodory's theorem and deletion of redundant members give normals `u_1,...,u_m`, `2<=m<=d+1`, and positive numbers `rho_j` such that

    sum_j rho_j u_j=0.

The closed halfspaces `{u_j.(x-y)>=0}` cover `R^d`, since their weighted margins sum to zero. Let one common sufficiently large exposing tilt `L` define

    H_j={u_j.(x-y)+L ell(z)>=0}.                     (4)

All off-base traces are strictly empty; on the own fiber the cuts and their cap masses are unchanged. Thus all are actual global depth-attaining caps, their continuous normals still balance, and their traces cover the whole `p`-fiber plane. The full ambient normals in (4) need not balance; no such assertion is needed or made.

Each cap's only nonzero section is the proper own section. By (3) its continuous centroid is `y`; its base coordinate is always `p`. Hence the full mixed section centroid is `Y`. The strict empty traces persist under small variations, so there are no other derivative or supporting-face terms. In particular, taking

    S_j=H_(d-1)(K_p intersect boundary H_j)/||u_j||,
    theta_j=(rho_j/S_j)/(sum_l rho_l/S_l)

gives the standard regular response profile. This proves part 3.

## 5. One actual localized potential pays every normalized critical profile

Choose a finite `B` large enough that for every off-base boundary point and every unit normal

    n.(x-y)+B ell(z)<0.

This is possible by compactness and strict base exposure. Define

    V(n,z,x)=[n.(x-y)+B ell(z)]_+.

For each fixed normal it is a nonnegative convex function of the physical variables, with continuous normal dependence. On other fiber normal bundles it vanishes. On the own boundary it is exactly `n.(x-y)>0`, because `y` is interior.

Gauss--Green gives

    integral V d eta=d|K_p|.

Every depth-attaining cap passes through `y` on the own fiber and captures exactly `Q`. Applying divergence to that proper cap gives

    integral_(boundary K_p intersect H_j) n.(x-y) dH_(d-1)=dQ.

The cut-plane flux is zero since `x-y` is tangent to that plane. The proper plane meets the own body boundary only in a surface-null set, so closed versus open cut conventions do not alter this boundary integral. Averaging with any `theta_j>=0`, `sum theta_j=1`, gives

    integral V W d eta=dQ.

Normalize `Phi=V/(d|K_p|)` to obtain (1). All off-base modifications or boundary allocations are annihilated pointwise. This proves part 4.

## 6. Boundary and global scope

The result covers `n=0` and singleton base sets by omitting the unnecessary localization term. It covers `d=1` with counting boundary measure and the ordinary interval midpoint. Empty fibers are omitted from `P`; all retained fibers are positive and full-dimensional in the common continuous space. No statement about varying lower-dimensional fiber directions is inferred.

When `d=0`, the depth-isolation assertion reduces to the counting identity `D_S(p)=1` at an exposed base. The boundary-potential construction is not defined and is not asserted in that case.

At exposed deepest bases, the individual potential obligation is therefore completely paid, including its regular-circuit interface. The unresolved geometric question is whether the nonexposed deepest face witnesses admit the same payment or can be replaced by a compatible paying family. Nothing here assumes such a replacement or identifies a finite witness count with the number of all critical circuits.

## 7. Exact transfer from any exposed base face

Let `F` be an exposed face of `conv P`, let `P_F=P intersect F`, and let `S_F` be the corresponding family, retaining its original fibers and measure. Choose an affine exposing functional `ell_F` that is zero on `F` and strictly negative on `P\F`. If there are no off-face bases, omit all localization terms.

For every `Y` over `F`,

    D_S(Y)=D_(S_F)(Y),                               (5)

where the latter allows all halfspaces of `aff(F) times R^d`. For one direction, restriction of an ambient containing halfspace is a containing relative halfspace or the whole relative space. For the converse, extend a relative affine halfspace functional to the ambient space and add `L ell_F(z)`. A finite sufficiently large `L` strictly removes all off-face fibers, while leaving the face trace exactly unchanged. Compactness and finiteness justify the finite choice of `L` just as in Section 2. This proves (5), without moving any base or changing any measure.

If a global deepest point lies over `F`, it is therefore a deepest point of `S_F` with the same raw depth `Q`. Any actual global depth-attaining cap captures exactly `Q` on `S_F` and zero volume off the face. Conversely, any local attaining cap can be extended by a sufficiently large finite exposing tilt to an actual global attaining cap strictly missing every other fiber.

There is also exact potential transfer. Suppose `phi(n,z,x)` is a finite nonnegative normal-dependent convex potential on `aff(F) times R^d`, jointly continuous (it is enough to assume uniform boundedness on the compact sets used below). Let `pi:R^n -> aff(F)` be an affine projection equal to the identity on `aff(F)`. Define

    Phi(n,z,x)=[phi(n,pi(z),x)+B ell_F(z)]_+.         (6)

For every fixed normal this is convex and nonnegative in the physical variables. Finite `P`, compact fibers, and the stated boundedness give a finite `B` for which it vanishes on every off-face normal bundle. On the face it equals `phi` exactly. Thus, for any profile `W` whose restriction there is `W_F`,

    integral Phi d eta=integral phi d eta_F,
    integral Phi W d eta=integral phi W_F d eta_F.    (7)

This remains true for profiles with supporting-face allocations: every off-face value is multiplied by zero; all on-face values are preserved rather than silently replaced. A local positive denominator stays positive, and every local efficiency transfers without loss.

The affine projection in (6) is only composition of a function, not a transformation of the lattice, the body, or the measure. No lattice-preserving property of that projection is needed. Likewise (5) retains every closed-boundary trace and makes no replacement of an atomic base measure by an integral.

This reduces a face witness to its actual face subfamily. It supplies no automatic efficiency for a positive-dimensional face and no claim that all deepest witnesses are exposed vertices of the full base hull.
